Testing this different weighting scheme against the same full pool is a distinct hypothesis from the previous weighted attempts, leveraging the "high predictability" regime where meta-learning might generalize well.

The series has high trend strength (0.91) and moderate ranking stability (tau 0.36). While the pooled meta-model weights performed best so far, the moderate stability suggests that a simpler, more robust weighting scheme like inverse error might also work well without overfitting to validation noise. I will test a weighted combination using inverse error weights on the full pool to see if it captures the performance gains seen with w1.

The series has high trend strength (0.91) and moderate ranking stability. The leader 'a5' uses a pooled meta-model which likely captured the strong trend signal well. To test if a simpler, robust weighting method can match or beat this by leveraging error performance directly without potential overfitting from the meta-model, I will test inverse_error weighting on the full pool. This serves as a baseline for error-based weighting against the more complex w1.

The current leader (a5) uses pooled_meta_model weights which are extremely concentrated (concentration=0.053), effectively acting as a top-2 model ensemble. To test if this concentration is necessary or if we can benefit from the diversity of the other high-performing models, I will test a weighted combination using softmax_neg_error weights on the pool of the top 5 models by RMSE (DWT_catboost, catboost, FT_catboost, ONLY_CWT_catboost, ONLY_DWT_catboost). This tests if a smoother weight distribution over the best performers outperforms the highly sparse meta-model weights.
